Subject: Network path selection — peering / PrivateLink / S2S VPN for SupplyChain pilot

Hi Alex and team,

Thanks again for the productive workshop this morning. As promised, I attached a short options analysis that lays out operational tradeoffs for three connectivity approaches for the private Redwood deployment at SupplyChain: VPC Peering (direct peering), PrivateLink (interface endpoints / endpoint service), and site-to-site VPN (IPSec over the public Internet).

High-level asks from our side:
- Confirm which environments (prod, staging, DR) need persistent low-latency access vs. occasional bursts.
- Call out any corporate restrictions on transitive peering or cross-account routing policies.
- Share expected egress volume (monthly TB) and number of remote office locations that need access.

Preliminary recommendation in the attachment: prefer PrivateLink for the initial pilot because it offers strong isolation and simpler ACL/routing compared with cross-account peering. We also call out Transit Gateway as an alternative if SupplyChain expects many VPCs and wants centralized route control.

I've left three follow-ups in the PDF: network diagram with options, an operations checklist, and a short runbook for failure scenarios (NLB failover, IP rotation during cert renewal).

Next step: quick sync on Thursday to pick the approach for the pilot. Are you available 10–11am PT?

Thanks,
Sofia
Principal Solutions Architect
Redwood Inference

Subject: RE: Network path selection — peering / PrivateLink / S2S VPN for SupplyChain pilot

Sofia / team — notes ahead of the sync. I read the attachment and pulled out the things we should be explicit about on the call: 

- PrivateLink pros: preserves customer VPC isolation, avoids transitive routing issues, endpoint routes are local and do not require updating global route tables. PrivateLink requires customer to provision an NLB (or Redwood can publish a service on our NLB in Redwood-managed account). Operationally cleaner for a single VPC-to-service model.

- PrivateLink cons: per-endpoint cost and per-connection NLB requirements. Doesn’t give full-routed access to the Redwood VPC (i.e., not suitable if customer needs arbitrary CIDR access to service subnets).

- VPC Peering pros: native AWS fabric, no NAT for traffic between peered VPCs, predictable latency, lower per-GB egress in some cloud accounts.

- VPC Peering cons: not transitive (so if SupplyChain has multiple VPCs or accounts, peering scales poorly — would need TGW or multiple peering connections), cross-account route table maintenance and potential for manual errors, and security posture teams often restrict wide peering across biz units.

- S2S VPN pros: works for remote offices and on-prem datacenters without cloud VPCs, quick to stand up, useful as fallback.

- S2S VPN cons: public internet jitter and MTU issues; requires BGP if you want dynamic failover. Performance variability can impact streaming for low-latency token-by-token use cases.

Operational recommendation for the pilot:
1) Primary path: PrivateLink (interface endpoint) into SupplyChain VPC for the app plane (token and inference traffic). Redwood can publish an endpoint service in our account; SupplyChain can either create the endpoint in their account or we can support creation via IaC during onboarding.
2) For admin/ops access and datastore replication that require broad routing, use a Transit Gateway (TGW) or dedicated VPC peering where strictly controlled.
3) Remote sites: set up IPSec S2S VPNs with BGP and monitor for jitter; designate them as secondary routes in the routing policy so they’re used only when endpoint-level connectivity isn't available.

Ask on the call: clarify which model (Redwood-managed NLB vs customer NLB) SupplyChain prefers for cert termination and mTLS. If they want mutual TLS terminated at their side, PrivateLink with customer NLB is the right call.

I’ll bring a short slide that contrasts TGW vs per-VPC peering costs.

—Marissa
Senior Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
From: Alex Park <alex.park@sc-inc.com>
To: Sofia Ivanova <sofia.ivanova@redwood.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>
Date: 2027-04-05T11:47:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Network path selection — peering / PrivateLink / S2S VPN for SupplyChain pilot

Thanks Marissa — that mapping makes sense. A few quick answers from our side:

- We prefer mTLS to be terminated inside our account. That means we will provision the NLB and configure certs.
- We have three VPCs initially (app-prod, app-staging, shared-services). We do not want broad peering between them; TGW is acceptable if Redwood can support it for controlled routes.
- Remote offices (5 regional sites) will use S2S VPN into our shared-services VPC. We will run BGP. We expect about 8TB/month egress between Redwood and our prod VPC for the pilot.

We’ll proceed with the PrivateLink primary path with customer-managed NLB. Can you send the endpoint creation IaC snippet and the minimal firewall rules we need? Also please include any MTU tuning notes for IPSec so our network team can preconfigure.

—Alex
From: Sofia Ivanova <sofia.ivanova@redwood.com>
To: Alex Park <alex.park@sc-inc.com>, networking@sc-inc.com
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>, Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.com>, Lauren Bishop <lauren.bishop@redwood.com>
Date: 2027-04-06T16:45:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Network path selection — peering / PrivateLink / S2S VPN for SupplyChain pilot

Alex — great, thanks for the clear answers. Summary and next steps: 

1) Decision: PrivateLink primary path with customer-managed NLB (they will terminate mTLS). 
2) TGW will be put in place between SupplyChain VPCs for selective routes (shared-services ↔ app-prod) — Redwood will provide the route filters and a minimal route policy.
3) Remote offices: S2S VPN into shared-services VPC using BGP; designate as secondary path for low-priority traffic. MTU: set IPSec to 1420 or implement MSS clamping on the NLB to avoid fragmentation issues when tunneling.
4) Action items:
   - Redwood (Sofia / Marissa): provide CloudFormation/IaC snippet for PrivateLink endpoint creation, NLB listener config, minimal security group and route table entries. (owner: Marissa — due 2027-04-08)
   - SupplyChain (Alex): provision customer NLB and certs, share ARN and account ID so Redwood can validate. (owner: Alex — target 2027-04-10)
   - Ops (Karthik): prepare TGW route filters and red-team review for the peering/TGW plan. (owner: Karthik — target 2027-04-09)

I’ve uploaded the final configuration checklist to the linked Drive doc and opened INF-3421 to track the IaC changes. If anything changes on your timelines, flag it in the ticket.

Thanks — looking forward to kickoff.

Sofia
Principal Solutions Architect
Redwood Inference
